body: @BenjaminAster  May I work on this issue?
@arya-vats Of course you may! After all, this is an open community where everyone can work on everything.

Saving a document as a PDF can be surprisingly complex for the average end user, so I think this is desparately needed. I like the idea of ```window.print({ saveAsPDF: true });```, but there should also be an option to change the default print settings, such as "Landscape" for layout, enabling "Background graphics" and the ability to change scale and margins.
As an alternative to passing print options, would it make sense to specify them via CSS using [Paged Media](https://www.w3.org/TR/css-page-3/) where all these (and much more) are already specified?

@mbrevda Ok, you're absolutely right! I've never looked into `@page` before, but yes, it seems all those things can actually already be done with just pure CSS. Size and layout can be controlled via `size`, margins via `margin`, the headers and footers can be hidden by setting the `@page` margin to 0 (and then giving the body a margin manually with `@media print`), and background graphics can be enabled via the `print-color-adjust: exact` CSS property (Chromium needs a `-webkit-` prefix here).

So I guess the `settings` option would actually be redundant here.

One thing that was brought up was the ability to not convert the entire page to PDF, but just a subsection of it, for example, for printing receipts: ```html

Receipt

``` If there were a way to pass a selector like `.receipt`, the user could create a PDF from only a subsection.

@tomayac This can already be done (with a bit of effort) by re-layouting the whole page with `@media print {}` (as described in my [Chromium Monorail comment](https://bugs.chromium.org/p/chromium/issues/detail?id=1012078#c6)) so that one element (in this case the `<section class="receipt">`) fills in the whole page, and everything else (in this case the app UI elements) gets a `display: none`.

But yes, I agree that it would be convenient to specify an element that gets printed individually and without some hacky CSS solution. Maybe something like `window.print({ saveAsPDF: true, selector: "section.receipt" })`?

It would be useful to be able to edit the metadata. For example as of now I think it's only possible to have the user agent as `Creator` and the moment you downloaded the pdf as `CreationDate`, which seems strange if the documents report another date.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/54818101/170707474-08fb7968-b633-4f17-9efc-5ea71784fae2.png)

Interesting - didn't know about ```print-color-adjust: exact``` and ```@page { size: landscape; }```, that's actually solving half my problems!

Instead of having a boolean, another option could be to just pass the HTML element into saveAsPDF.

```js
window.print({ saveAsPDF: document.body })
window.print({ saveAsPDF: document.querySelector('section.receipt') })
```

Agree, would make sense to be able to specify metadata when generating the PDF document. I guess the browser could just use the data already provided by HTML ```<meta>``` tags.

```<meta name="pdf:title" content="Receipt">``` could be used if the page generates a PDF from a subsection (as it would likely differ from the title of the HTML document).
To simplify the API surface, perhaps the ability to print could be added to any element, like `someSelector.saveAsPdf()`

> To simplify the API surface, perhaps the ability to print could be added to any element, like someSelector.saveAsPdf()

:+1:  In some situations it would be nice to have the ability to get the printed PDF file programmatically
Any updates on this functionality? would be very useful

A bit of context about the referenced issue (now closed). This proposal was a bit different, as it suggested adding an API that would generate a PDF as an `ArrayBuffer`, which would lead to security issues. This was pointed out by @annevk in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/10612#issuecomment-2360168230:
> This isn't viable for the same reason we don't support screenshots. That would leak information about what is displayed on the page.

@annevk Could you provide some thoughts on if the proposal in this issue might be considered viable with the following boundaries:
- Scripts do not get access to the generated PDF, its contents or its file handle.
- The UA generates the PDF and shows the save dialog.
- Optional: user activation is required.

I would also like to add my two cents regarding the API and provide some motivation mentioned earlier by @apurvaojas in #10612, supplemented with my own views for completeness.

## What problem are you trying to solve?
Web developers often need to generate a PDF representation of their content. Generating a PDF from a web page today is primarily achieved through the `window.print()` API, which requires user interaction (via a print dialog) to save the page as a PDF. Exporting as PDF through this approach is suboptimal and results in poor UX for end users, because sometimes downloading as PDF is the intention, not printing. Furthermore, this always targets the entire document and always applies print styles. This is useful for end-user printing, but it is not sufficient for common scenarios such as:
- Exporting a specific subsection of a page (e.g. a receipt, invoice, or report component).
- Producing a PDF with the screen styling (e.g. branded documents that should match the on-screen look, not the print stylesheet).
- Controlling suggested and/or definitive PDF output options (page size, orientation, margins, scaling) when print styles are not applied.

## What solutions exist today?
Developers currently have to resort to custom solutions and hacks, such as: 
- Server-side PDF generation using third-party libs or rendering a web page to PDF using a headless browser like Puppeteer
- Client-side PDF generation using third-party libs, like jsPDF/PDF.js/pdfkit, along with a `<iframe>` + `window.print()` hack

These third-party libs, especially when used client-side, have big disadvantages:
- Inconsistency across browsers
- Significant performance and rendering issues, especially with large or complex pages
- They can be overly complex when generating PDFs from dynamic, styled content
- Limited support for maintaining CSS and layout fidelity
- Complex setup and additional dependencies
- Increased bundle size / downloaded bytes

The current methods do not provide a native, efficient way to export a web page or specific parts of it as a PDF programmatically, leading to fragmentation and varied developer experience across applications and platforms. A standardized client-side API would improve consistency, interoperability and remove the need for heavy workarounds.

Therefore, this proposal has the following goals:
1. Allow saving a page or a specific subsection of a page (e.g. a receipt, invoice, or report component) directly to PDF.
2. Allow producing a PDF with the print or screen styling applied (e.g. for branded documents that should match the on-screen look, not the print stylesheet).
3. Optional: controlling suggested and/or definitive PDF output options (page size, orientation, margins, scaling) when print styles are not applied.

## How would you solve it?
A better DX and UX could be achieved by adding a new Web API method, either on the `window` object or under a `navigator` namespace object like `navigator.export` (if "export" would not cause any problems or confusion with ESM modules at least). This method will allow developers to programmatically generate a PDF of a web page or specified DOM elements, showing a save file dialog, so the PDF can be saved to disk directly. The API can leverage the browser's built-in PDF generation (the same functionality used by `window.print()`) whenever print styles should be applied and the entire web page is exported to PDF. For any other scenarios, I am open to suggestions and ideas from the community and specialists on the topic.

#### Key features of the proposed API:
- **Programmatic PDF generation and save capability:** The API will trigger the UA to generate a PDF and show a save file dialog. It returns a `Promise` resolving with `undefined` or rejecting with a `DOMException`, such as `AbortError` or `SecurityError`.
- **Native performance:** The API will use native browser capabilities, ensuring faster and more reliable PDF generation compared to third-party libraries.

The proposed method would be available under `window` or a `navigator` namespace object. I have the following suggestions:
- `navigator.download.asPdf` (see: https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/4148)
- `navigator.export.saveAsPdf`
- `navigator.export.asPdf`
- `window.saveAsPdf`

I lean towards `navigator.download.asPdf`, as the `navigator.download` namespace could later accommodate other possibly interesting export targets (e.g. `asText`, or `asImage` for programmatically taken screenshots of a page or sections of it), and the underlying functionality is essentially unrelated to printing.

The method would take an optional options object, that shares some options with File System Access API's [`showSaveFilePicker`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/showSaveFilePicker) method:
- `target` (optional)
  - An [`Element`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Element) to generate a PDF for. Defaults to `document.documentElement`.
- `suggestedName` (optional)
  - A [String](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String). The suggested file name.
- `startIn` (optional)
  - A [FileSystemHandle](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/FileSystemHandle) or a well known directory (`"desktop"`, `"documents"`, `"downloads"`, `"music"`, `"pictures"`, or `"videos"`) to open the dialog in.
- `cssMedia` (optional)
  - `"print"` or `"screen"`, stating what CSS media's styles to apply. Defaults to `"print"`. When `cssMedia` is `"screen"`, `@media print` styles are ignored entirely. The document is rendered as if no print stylesheet exists.

Up for debate is what the exact return value should be. `window.showSaveFilePicker` behaves as follows:
- Return `Promise`
- Resolves the promise with a `FileSystemFileHandle`
- Rejects the promise with `AbortError` when dismissed
- Rejects the promise with `SecurityError` in several scenarios (e.g. see: https://wicg.github.io/file-system-access/#local-file-system-permissions) 

However, I don't think we need a `FileSystemFileHandle` in the discussed API, so our return signature could be `Promise<void>`, I think.

#### Example:
```js
// Promise<void>, could reject with DOMException
await navigator.download.asPdf({
  target: document.documentElement,
  suggestedName: 'invoice.pdf',
  startIn: 'downloads',
  cssMedia: 'print',
});
```

## Anything else?
### Security
This method should probably require transient activation, just like `window.showSaveFilePicker`. If called without user activation, it would throw a `SecurityError` `DOMException`.

t.b.d. — Any input from experts is greatly appreciated!

I'm particularly curious about the following situations:
- When a `FileSystemHandle` is passed to `startIn`, it would in theory be possible for the script to read the file immediately after saving, since a directory handle retains its permissions. This would be insecure. This conflicts with the "scripts get no access to the generated PDF" boundary. A possible mitigation: only accept `WellKnownDirectory` enum values for `startIn`, not handles, keeping the start-location hint without the option to read immediately afterwards.
- When the script did not use `startIn`, but has requested and received access to the directory the exported PDF has been downloaded into using the File System Access API, this might be a security issue too.

### Current UA PDF generation capabilities
As I'm not an expert on the topic, I'd like to know if rendering a DOM element other than `document.documentElement` is currently possible in any of the major browsers.

### CSS `print` vs. `screen` styles
I'm curious to hear thoughts on whether the API should and could allow exporting to PDF while applying the `screen` styles, instead of `print` styles. I'm aware I haven't fully thought this through and it could be a future enhancement, let me know your thoughts! It is currently unclear to me whether UAs can render an arbitrary DOM element in isolation with screen styles applied. Feedback from browser implementors on feasibility is welcome.

### Progressive enhancements
To keep the initial scope minimal, the whole-document + print-styles case (essentially `window.print()` without the print-dialog detour) could land first, with `target` and `cssMedia: "screen"` as progressive enhancements.

Is this proposal still actively being considered? I run into this limitation frequently when building stuff and the current workarounds (like server-side generation or complex print stylesheets) are very brittle for users. I'd love to see the API proposed by @Anoesj move forward. Is there anything the community can do to help demonstrate implementer interest?

I don't think it's actively considered right now, but that can always change. I think what @Anoesj proposed makes sense. The one thing that's giving me pause is that we haven't really figured out a minimal download API (#4148) yet (if we ignore the `download` attribute) and this would essentially be a special case of that.
